sophia: Hey perf folks — seeing a regression in p99 for small-batch KV lookups after the kernel-selector change. Trying nsys but outputs are huge and I'm not seeing the tiny kernels that spike latency around evictions. Any recommended CLI flags / workflow for capturing CUDA + OSRT + NVTX focused on KV cache evict hotspots?

mike: For this class of issues I do short, targeted captures with NVTX brackets. Key points: 1) bracket only the region (warm + critical section) 2) keep duration small to avoid huge qdrep files 3) enable osrt to see runtime queues. Example I use below.

mike: ```bash
# quick targeted capture around NVTX markers (warm loop outside)
nsys profile --output=kv-evict-test --trace=cuda,nvtx,osrt \
  --capture-range=nvtx:start:stop --sample=cpu --force-overwrite --duration=20
```

arya: A couple of extras: 1) if kernels are sub-ms, sampling may miss them — switch to more repeats and shorter per-run duration rather than one long capture. 2) add `--sample=none` and rely on full tracing for very short runs if file size is acceptable. 3) capture the host threads too so you can correlate scheduler delays.

sophia: What about sample settings? I saw docs mentioning sampling frequency but CLI options seemed fuzzy.

mike: Right — nsys sampling is a tradeoff. You can increase sample density by reducing the sampling period, e.g., `--sample=cpu:100us` (if available on your nsys build). If you can't, do many short runs with NVTX to aggregate events. Also consider `--capture-range=pid:<pid>` when you only want the process's timeline.

lucas: If qdrep size is the blocker, try: 1) `--output=kv-evict-test.qdrep` but then immediately run `nsys export` or `nsys stats` to extract CSV/JSON reports and discard the big file. 2) Use `--trace=cuda,osrt` (drop nvtx) for a smaller but still useful view.

lucas: Quick commands: ```bash
# export a lighter summary report and flame graph CSVs
nsys stats -f report.csv kv-evict-test.qdrep
nsys export --export=timeline --output=kv-evict-test-timeline.json kv-evict-test.qdrep
```

sophia: Good tips. I'm also worried sampling bias: the eviction path is rare but expensive. Any advice to amplify it?

arya: Create a synthetic workload that forces evictions (smaller cache + adversarial keys), then NVTX-bracket the evict function and collect multiple runs. That gives better signal-to-noise. Also tag branches inside the runtime (e.g., `NVTX_PUSH("evict-start")`) so you can use `--capture-range=nvtx:evict-start:evict-end`.

mike: In the UI look for these things: 1) kernel occupancy dips right before spike 2) ASYNC API events queued but long host-side gaps 3) OSRT queue threads (look for heavy scheduling on runtime thread). Use the timeline's `CUDA API` lanes + `Threads` lanes to correlate.

perf-bot: Tip: when you run many short captures, label outputs with the commit + trial id so you can bulk-compare: `kv-evict-$(git rev-parse --short HEAD)-run-01.qdrep`.

sophia: Thanks — I'll: (a) add NVTX brackets around evict path, (b) run many 10-15s captures with smaller cache to force evicts, (c) export reports to CSV and diff the kernel durations. Will post one qdrep if I still can't find the hotspot. :thumbsup:

mike: If you post a qdrep, include the `nsys stats` summary and an exported timeline JSON. For quick triage I'll look for one of these patterns: repeated tiny kernels that line up with a host sleep, or big memcpy kernels right after eviction markers.

sophia: Will do — thanks all!
